maths.s: Treating zero as a number in its own right, with rules for adding, subtracting and multiplying, was developed in India.
maths.e: Brahmagupta set out rules for calculating with zero in 628 AD. The concept travelled through the Islamic world to Europe.

maths.s: There are more ways to order a shuffled deck of 52 cards than there are atoms on Earth.
maths.e: 52! is about 8 × 10⁶⁷, far more than the roughly 10⁵⁰ atoms on Earth. A well-shuffled deck is almost certainly in an order never seen before.

maths.s: In a room of just 23 people, there's about a 50% chance that two of them share a birthday.
maths.e: This is the birthday paradox. With 23 people there are 253 possible pairs, and with 70 people the chance rises above 99.9%.

maths.s: 0.999… (with the 9s repeating forever) is slightly less than 1.
maths.e: 0.999… is exactly equal to 1. For example, 1/3 = 0.333…, and three times that is 0.999… = 3/3 = 1.

maths.s: Fibonacci numbers appear in nature, for example in the spirals of sunflower seeds.
maths.e: Sunflower heads and pine cones often have 34 and 55, or 55 and 89, spirals in each direction. These are consecutive Fibonacci numbers.

maths.s: The digits of pi eventually repeat in a pattern.
maths.e: Pi is irrational: its decimal expansion never ends and never falls into a repeating pattern. It has been computed to trillions of digits.

maths.s: There are infinitely many prime numbers, which was proven over 2,000 years ago.
maths.e: Euclid's elegant proof: multiply any finite list of primes together and add 1. The result has a prime factor that isn't on the list.

maths.s: All infinite sets are the same size.
maths.e: Georg Cantor proved that some infinities are bigger than others. For example, there are more real numbers than whole numbers.

maths.s: In theory, folding a sheet of paper in half 42 times would make it thick enough to reach the Moon.
maths.e: Doubling 0.1 mm 42 times gives about 440,000 km, more than the 384,000 km to the Moon. In practice, paper can't be folded that many times.

maths.s: A 'googol' is 1 followed by 100 zeros, and it inspired the name Google.
maths.e: The word was coined in 1920 by a nine-year-old, the nephew of mathematician Edward Kasner. Google's founders adapted the spelling.

maths.s: In the Monty Hall problem, switching doors doubles your chance of winning the car.
maths.e: Your first pick wins 1/3 of the time, so switching wins 2/3 of the time. Many mathematicians refused to believe it at first.

maths.s: Srinivasa Ramanujan, a largely self-taught mathematician from India, produced nearly 3,900 results.
maths.e: He worked with G. H. Hardy at Cambridge. Mathematicians are still exploring the formulas in his notebooks.

maths.s: The equals sign (=) was invented in 1557.
maths.e: Welsh mathematician Robert Recorde introduced it because 'no two things can be more equal' than a pair of parallel lines.

maths.s: A circle has 360 degrees because of a law of nature.
maths.e: 360 is a convention, probably inherited from Babylonian astronomy and its base-60 number system. Mathematicians often use radians instead.

maths.s: Fermat's Last Theorem remained unproven for more than 350 years.
maths.e: Pierre de Fermat claimed a proof in a margin in 1637. Andrew Wiles finally proved it in 1994.

beliefs.s: Christianity and Islam are the two largest religions in the world by number of followers.
beliefs.e: Christianity has around 2.3 billion followers and Islam around 1.9 billion. Hinduism is third, with over 1 billion.

beliefs.s: Hinduism is often described as the oldest living major religion, with roots more than 3,000 years old.
beliefs.e: Its earliest texts, the Vedas, were composed more than 3,000 years ago. Hinduism has no single founder.

beliefs.s: Some Jain monks sweep the ground in front of them as they walk, to avoid harming insects.
beliefs.e: Jainism teaches ahimsa, non-violence towards all living beings, so strictly that many Jains avoid root vegetables to spare tiny organisms.

beliefs.s: The Golden Temple in Amritsar serves free meals to tens of thousands of people every day.
beliefs.e: Its langar, a community kitchen run largely by volunteers, feeds anyone regardless of religion, caste or background. Everyone sits together on the floor.

beliefs.s: Buddhists worship the Buddha as an all-powerful creator god.
beliefs.e: The Buddha was a human teacher, Siddhartha Gautama, who taught a path to end suffering. Buddhism does not centre on a creator god.

beliefs.s: Shinto, Japan's indigenous religion, has no single founder and no single holy book.
beliefs.e: Shinto centres on kami, spirits found in nature, places and ancestors, and is practised at about 80,000 shrines.

beliefs.s: Zoroastrianism, one of the world's oldest religions, is still practised by the Parsi community in India.
beliefs.e: Parsis migrated from Persia to India over a thousand years ago. Famous Parsis include the Tata family and Freddie Mercury.

beliefs.s: Judaism, Christianity and Islam are called 'Abrahamic religions'.
beliefs.e: All three trace their origins to the figure of Abraham and share many prophets and stories.

beliefs.s: During Ramadan, many Muslims fast from dawn until sunset for about a month.
beliefs.e: The fast is broken each evening with a meal called iftar. Ramadan ends with the celebration of Eid al-Fitr.

beliefs.s: The Bahá'í Faith, founded in 19th-century Persia, teaches the unity of all religions.
beliefs.e: Its world centre, with famous terraced gardens, is in Haifa and Acre in Israel.

beliefs.s: Many people in Japan take part in both Shinto and Buddhist traditions.
beliefs.e: A common saying is that people are born Shinto and die Buddhist: births are celebrated at shrines, while funerals are usually Buddhist.

beliefs.s: 'Atheist' and 'agnostic' mean exactly the same thing.
beliefs.e: An atheist doesn't believe in any god. An agnostic holds that whether gods exist is unknown or unknowable. Some people are both.

beliefs.s: Lalibela in Ethiopia has 11 medieval churches carved out of solid rock.
beliefs.e: Carved downward into the ground around the 12th and 13th centuries, they are still active places of worship.

beliefs.s: Angkor Wat, the largest religious monument in the world, was first built as a Hindu temple.
beliefs.e: Built in the 12th century and dedicated to Vishnu, it gradually became a Buddhist temple. It appears on Cambodia's flag.

ethics.s: The 'trolley problem' asks whether it's right to divert a runaway trolley so it kills one person instead of five.
ethics.e: Philosophers and psychologists use it to explore when, if ever, it's acceptable to harm one person to save more.

ethics.s: Versions of the 'Golden Rule' (treat others as you want to be treated) appear in many religions and philosophies worldwide.
ethics.e: It appears in Confucianism, Hinduism, Buddhism, Judaism, Christianity and Islam, among others.

ethics.s: Utilitarianism judges actions by whether they produce the greatest good for the greatest number.
ethics.e: Developed by Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill, it's the basis for many cost–benefit decisions in public policy.

ethics.s: Socrates wrote many books setting out his philosophy.
ethics.e: Socrates wrote nothing. We know his ideas mainly through his students, especially Plato.

ethics.s: The 'Ship of Theseus' puzzle asks whether an object that has had every part replaced is still the same object.
ethics.e: The question applies to everything from bands with no original members to the human body, whose cells are constantly replaced.

ethics.s: Confucius taught that a harmonious society depends on proper relationships, such as respect for parents and elders.
ethics.e: Confucian ideas about family, education and good government have shaped East Asian cultures for over 2,000 years.

ethics.s: The Southern African philosophy of 'Ubuntu' is often summed up as 'I am because we are'.
ethics.e: Ubuntu stresses community, compassion and shared humanity. It was often cited by Nelson Mandela and Desmond Tutu.

ethics.s: Philosopher Peter Singer argued that if you'd ruin your shoes to save a drowning child, you should also give to save distant strangers.
ethics.e: His 1972 essay 'Famine, Affluence, and Morality' helped inspire the effective altruism movement.

ethics.s: Kant argued that lying is wrong even to a murderer asking where your friend is hiding.
ethics.e: Kant held that moral duties like honesty don't depend on consequences, a view still debated today.

ethics.s: Machiavelli advised rulers to always be kind and honest.
ethics.e: In The Prince (1532), Machiavelli wrote that it's safer for a ruler to be feared than loved, and that deception can be necessary.

ethics.s: John Rawls asked people to design a fair society without knowing which position in it they would end up in.
ethics.e: Rawls called this the 'veil of ignorance'. He argued it would lead people to protect the worst-off.

ethics.s: Stoic philosophers such as Marcus Aurelius taught people to focus on what is within their control.
ethics.e: Marcus Aurelius, a Roman emperor, wrote his Stoic reflections in a private journal now known as Meditations.

ethics.s: The Arthashastra is an ancient Indian treatise on statecraft, economics and military strategy.
ethics.e: It's traditionally attributed to Chanakya (Kautilya), adviser to the Maurya Empire's founder.

games.e: Its ancestor, chaturanga, was played in India around the 6th century AD. The game spread through Persia to the Arab world and Europe.

games.s: There are more possible chess games than atoms in the observable universe.
games.e: Claude Shannon estimated about 10¹²⁰ possible games, compared with about 10⁸⁰ atoms in the observable universe.

games.s: Basketball was invented by a Canadian.
games.e: James Naismith, a Canadian-born teacher, invented it in 1891 in Springfield, Massachusetts, using peach baskets as hoops.

games.s: An astronaut has hit golf balls on the Moon.
games.e: Alan Shepard hit two golf balls on the Moon during Apollo 14 in 1971, using a club head attached to a sample-collection tool.

games.s: Kabaddi, a fast contact sport where a raider must hold their breath while chanting, originated in ancient India.
games.e: It's Bangladesh's national sport and is hugely popular across South Asia, with professional leagues.

games.s: According to tradition, the ancient Olympic Games began in 776 BC.
games.e: They were held every four years at Olympia in honour of Zeus, for over 1,000 years.

games.s: Tug of war has never been an Olympic sport.
games.e: Tug of war was part of the Olympic Games from 1900 to 1920.

games.s: An AI first beat a top professional player at the board game Go in 2016.
games.e: DeepMind's AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol 4–1. Go has so many possible positions that this was expected to take another decade.

games.s: A Test cricket match can last up to five days and still end in a draw.
games.e: Test cricket is the longest format of the sport. A draw happens when time runs out before a result is reached.

games.s: Sepak takraw is like volleyball, but players can only use their feet, knees, chest and head.
games.e: It's popular across Southeast Asia, and players perform acrobatic overhead kicks to spike the ball.

games.s: Snakes and ladders originated in ancient India as a game about morality.
games.e: Called Moksha Patam, it used ladders to represent virtues and snakes to represent vices. British players brought it to Europe.

games.s: Tetris was created by a Soviet software engineer in 1984.
games.e: Alexey Pajitnov developed it in Moscow. Its name combines 'tetra' (four, the number of squares in each piece) and tennis, his favourite sport.

games.s: The first modern Olympic Games were held in Paris in 1896.
games.e: They were held in Athens in 1896, honouring the ancient Greek games. Paris hosted the second, in 1900.

games.s: A Rubik's Cube has over 43 quintillion possible positions.
games.e: That's 43,252,003,274,489,856,000 positions. Hungarian inventor Ernő Rubik created the cube in 1974.

games.s: Any scrambled Rubik's Cube can be solved in 20 moves or fewer.
games.e: This was proved in 2010 using about 35 CPU-years of donated computer time. The number is nicknamed 'God's Number'.
games.w: Optimal solutions for the Rubik's Cube

arts.s: Beethoven composed his Ninth Symphony when he was almost completely deaf.
arts.e: At its premiere in 1824, Beethoven reportedly had to be turned around to see the audience applauding.

arts.s: The Taj Mahal was built by Emperor Shah Jahan in memory of his wife Mumtaz Mahal.
arts.e: Construction began in 1632 and involved around 20,000 workers. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

arts.s: The Statue of Liberty was designed and built in the United States.
arts.e: It was a gift from France, designed by Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi with an iron framework engineered by Gustave Eiffel, built in Paris and shipped in pieces.

arts.s: India produces more feature films each year than any other country.
arts.e: India produces well over 1,500 films a year in many languages: Bollywood (Hindi), Tollywood (Telugu), Kollywood (Tamil) and more.

arts.s: In Indian classical music, many ragas are traditionally linked to particular times of day.
arts.e: A raga is a melodic framework for improvisation. Some are meant for dawn, others for evening or night, and some for particular seasons.

arts.s: The Mona Lisa was stolen from the Louvre in 1911.
arts.e: An Italian handyman, Vincenzo Peruggia, hid it for over two years. The theft made it the most famous painting in the world.

arts.s: Michelangelo painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling in just a few weeks.
arts.e: It took him about four years, from 1508 to 1512, working mostly standing up on scaffolding with his head tilted back.

arts.s: BTS were the first all-South Korean act to top the US Billboard Hot 100.
arts.e: Their song 'Dynamite' reached number 1 in 2020, a milestone in K-pop's global rise.

arts.s: Hokusai's 'The Great Wave off Kanagawa' is a woodblock print, so many original copies exist.
arts.e: Made around 1831, it was printed from carved wooden blocks. Thousands of impressions were made, and museums around the world own early ones.

arts.s: Mozart and Beethoven were close friends of the same age.
arts.e: Mozart was born in 1756 and Beethoven in 1770. They may have met briefly in Vienna in 1787, but they were never close friends.

arts.s: There is a famous piece of music in which the performers play no notes at all.
arts.e: In John Cage's 4′33″ (1952), the musicians sit silently, and the 'music' is the ambient sound of the room.

arts.s: The Terracotta Army includes around 8,000 life-size soldier figures, buried with China's first emperor.
arts.e: Farmers digging a well discovered it in 1974. Each soldier's face is different.

arts.s: Kintsugi is the Japanese art of repairing broken pottery with gold, highlighting the cracks rather than hiding them.
arts.e: It reflects the idea that breakage and repair are part of an object's history, not something to disguise.

arts.s: Reggae music originated in Jamaica in the late 1960s.
arts.e: Bob Marley brought reggae to the world, and UNESCO added it to its list of intangible cultural heritage in 2018.
